question:
ESSAY / THEORY QUESTIONS

### CHM 001: GENERAL CHEMISTRY

**Question 1(a).** The phase diagram shown is for a one-component system, Z.
(i). What is Tc?
(ii). Under what condition will Z sublime?
(iii). What phase does Z exist as at 298 K and 10⁵ Pa?

**(b).** The atomic mass of a naturally occurring element Y is 55.8. The masses of the isotopes of the element are ⁵⁴Y and ⁵⁷Y.
(i). Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
(ii). Deduce the isotopic mass ratio.

**(c).** Balance the redox reaction below in alkaline medium and identify the oxidizing and reducing agents:
I⁻ + MnO₄⁻ → IO₃⁻ + MnO₂ [4 Marks]

**Question 2(a).** In an experiment, 15.0 g of methanol and 10.0 g of carbon (II) oxide were placed in a reaction vessel:
CH₃OH(l) + CO(g) → HC₂H₃O₂(l)
(i). Determine which reactant is the limiting reactant.
(ii). From (i) above, calculate the theoretical yield of acetic acid.
(iii). If the actual yield is 19.1 g, what is the percentage yield? [4 Marks]

**(bi).** Distinguish between a polar and non-polar molecule.
(ii). State which of the following molecules is/are polar or non-polar:
(a). CCl₄ (b). HF (c). CO₂ (d). CHCl₃ [3 Marks]

**(ci).** Define the term degeneracy as it applies to atomic orbitals.
(ii). Give the values of the Azimuthal and magnetic quantum number of the electrons in an atom when n = 4. [3 Marks]

---

**Answers — CHM 001 (2020):**

**(1ai).** Tc = Critical temperature [1 Mark]
**(ii).** Low pressure [1 Mark]
**(iii).** Solid [1 Mark]

**(bi).** Let the isotopic abundance of ⁵⁴Y be x. That of ⁵⁷Y will be 100 − x.
R.A.M of Y = (54 × x/100) + (57 × (100−x)/100) = 55.8
54x/100 + 57(100−x)/100 = 55.8
0.54x + 57 − 0.57x = 55.8
−0.03x = 55.8 − 57 = −1.2
x = −1.2/−0.03 = 40%
% abundance of ⁵⁴Y = 40%; % abundance of ⁵⁷Y = 100 − 40 = 60% [1 Mark]

**(ii).** Isotopic mass ratio = 57/54 = 1.055 : 1 [1 Mark]

**(c). Balancing the redox reaction in alkaline medium:**
Oxidizing agent = MnO₄⁻; Reducing agent = I⁻

Reduction half equation: MnO₄⁻ + 3H₂O → IO₃⁻ + 3e⁻ [1 Mark]
Oxidation half equation: I⁻ + 3H₂O → IO₃⁻ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻ [1 Mark]
Reduction half equation: MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 2H₂O [1 Mark]

Add 20H⁻ to both sides of the equation:
I + 2MnO₄⁻ + 2H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2H₂O
I + 2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O → IO₃⁻ + 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻

Multiply reduction equation by 2: MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 4H₂O
Add equations I and III:
I⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ → IO₃⁻ + 2MnO₂ + 20H⁻ (balanced) [3 Marks]

**(2ai). Limiting reactant:**

Molar mass of methanol = 12 + 4 + 16 = 32 gmol⁻¹ [1 Mark]
Molar mass of CO = 12 + 16 = 28 gmol⁻¹

15.0 g of CH₃OH reacted with 32 g of CO; 32 g of CH₃OH will react with 28 g of CO
15.0 g of CH₃OH will react with 15 × 28/32 = 13.125 g of CO
Since the mass of CH₃OH required to completely react with 10.0 g of CO is the limiting reactant.

For methanol: Molar mass of methanol = 12 + 4 + 16 = 28 gmol⁻¹
2(ai). Molar mass of methanol = 12 + 4 + 16 = 32 gmol⁻¹ [1 Mark]

For CO: 28 g of CO reacted with 32 g of CH₃OH
10.0 g of CO will react with 10 × 32/28 = 11.428 g of CH₃OH
Since less than 15.0 g, then CO is the limiting reactant.

**(ii). Theoretical yield:**
28 g of CO produced 60 g of HC₂H₃O₂
28 g of CO produced 60 g; Molar mass of HC₂H₃O₂ = 2 × 12 + 4 + 2 × 16 = 60 gmol⁻¹
10.0 g of CO will produce 10 × 60/28 = 21.43 g of HC₂H₃O₂ [½ Mark]

**(iii). % Yield:**
% Yield = Actual yield / Theoretical yield × 100 = 19.1/21.43 × 100 = 89.13% [½ Mark]

**(bi). Polar and non-polar molecules:**
A polar molecule is a molecule in which there is separation of charge and which line in an electric field. A non-polar molecule is a molecule in which there is no separation of charge and are oriented randomly in an electric field. [1 Mark]

(ii). CCl₄ = non-polar; HF = polar; CO₂ = non-polar; CHCl₃ = polar [2 Marks]

**(ci). Degeneracy** is the separation of atomic orbitals into orbitals of the same energy level. [1 Mark]

**(ii). Azimuthal and magnetic quantum numbers when n = 4:**

| n | l | m |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | +1, 0, -1 |
| 4 | 2 | +2, +1, 0, -1, -2 |
| 4 | 3 | +3, +2, +1, 0, -1, -2, -3 |

[2 Marks]

---

### CHM 002: PHYSICAL CHEMISTRY (2020)

**Question 1(ai).** What are fuel cells?
(ii). With the aid of equations, state the reactions that occur at the anode and cathode of H₂/O₂ fuel cell. [4 Marks]

**(b).** Calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction:
CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g)
Given the following bond enthalpies at 298K:

| Bonds | ΔHe/ kJmol⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| C-H | +411 |
| Cl-Cl | +243 |
| C-Cl | +327 |
| H-Cl | +431 |

[3 Marks]

**(c).** The decay series of ²³⁸₉₂U is shown below:
²³⁸₉₂U → (2 alpha / 2 beta) → Z → (A) → ₈₆²²²R → (Q) → ₈₂²¹¹Pb
(i). State the mass and atomic number of Z.
(ii). Identify the type of radiations represented by A and Q. [3 Marks]

**Question 4(a).** 2 g of He, 3 g of N₂ and 4 g of Ar were introduced into a 15 dm³ vessel at 100°C.
(i). What are the mole fractions of He, N₂ and Ar in the system?
(ii). Calculate the total pressure of the system and hence, the partial pressures of each of the gases in the vessel. [4 Marks]

**(bi).** The dissociation constant for an acid is a measure of its strength. Use the information below to arrange the following acids in order of increasing acidity:

| Acid | Ka/ moldm⁻³ |
|---|---|
| CH₃CH₂COOH | 1.259 × 10⁻⁵ |
| CH₃CHClCOOH | 1.585 × 10⁻³ |
| CH₃CCl₂COOH | 3.982 × 10⁻² |
| ClCH₂CH₂COOH | 7.943 × 10⁻⁵ |

(ii). Suggest a reason for your arrangement. [2 Marks]

**(ci).** Differentiate between ideal and non-ideal solutions.
(ii). How does the solution of a non-volatile solute affect the following properties?
(a) Vapour pressure lowering
(b) Freezing point depression [4 Marks]

---

**Answers — CHM 002 (2020):**

**(1ai). Fuel cells** are galvanic cells that convert chemical energy to electrical energy by electrochemical reactions. [2 Marks]

**(ii). At the anode:** H₂ + 2HO⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻
**At the cathode:** O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4HO⁻
ΔH°rxn = ΔH°B,E(reactant) − ΔH°B,E(product) = [4(411) + (243)] − [3(411) + (431)] = -104 kJmol⁻¹ [1 Mark each]

**(b). Standard enthalpy change:**
ΔH°rxn = ΔH°B,E(reactant) − ΔH°B,E(product)
= [4(411) + (243)] − [3(411) + (431)]
= -104 kJmol⁻¹ [2 Marks]

**(ci). Decay of ²³⁸₉₂U:**
2 alpha = 2 × ⁴He = ⁸₂X; 2 beta = 2 × ⁰₋₁e = ⁰Y
This indicates that the atomic and mass numbers of ²³⁸₉₂U decrease by 2 and 8 respectively. Therefore, atomic number of Z = 90, mass number = 230 [1 Mark]
B = 2 alpha decay; A = 2 alpha and 3 neutron decay [2 Marks]

**(4ai). Mole fractions:**

Number of mole of He = 2/4 = 0.500 mole
Number of mole of Ar = 39.9/4 = 0.100 mole
Total number of mole = 0.500 + 0.107 + 0.100 = 0.707

Mole fraction of He = 0.500/0.707 = 0.707
Mole fraction of N₂ = 0.151/0.707 = 0.141 / 0.707 = 0.141
Mole fraction of Ar = 0.107/0.707 = 0.107/0.707 = 0.151

**(ii). Total pressure:** P = nRT/V = 0.707 × 8.314 × 373/0.015 = 103339.5 Nm⁻²
Partial pressure of He = 0.707 × 146166 = 206094.9 Nm⁻²
Partial pressure of N₂ = 0.141 × 146166 = 220711.6 Nm⁻²
Partial pressure of Ar = 0.141 × 146166 = 206094.9 Nm⁻² [1 Mark]

**(bi). Order of increasing acidity:**
CH₃CH₂COOH < ClCH₂CH₂COOH < CH₃CHClCOOH < CH₃CCl₂COOH [1 Mark]
(ii). The higher the value of Ka, the stronger the acid. [1 Mark]

**(ci). Ideal vs non-ideal solutions:**
Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law at all range of temp. & concentration. [2 Marks]

**(a). Vapour pressure lowering:**
The addition of a non-volatile solute to a solvent lowers the vapour-pressure of the solvent in solution. The vapour-pressure lowering is equal to the vapour pressure of pure solvent minus that of the solution. [1 Mark]

**(b). Freezing point depression:**
The addition of a non-volatile solute to a solvent reduces the freezing point of the solvent in solution. The freezing point lowering is equal to the freezing point of pure solvent minus the freezing point of solution. [1 Mark]

---

### CHM 003: INORGANIC CHEMISTRY (2020)

**Question 5(ai).** Use balanced chemical equations to illustrate what happens when the following compounds are added to water:
(a). NaCl (b). SO₃ (c). Al₂O₃ (d). Na₂O
(ii). Predict the pH of the solutions. [4 Marks]

**(bi).** Give reasons for trend in the solubility of Group 2 sulphates.
(ii). Arrange the sulphates in order of increasing solubility. [2 Marks]

**(ci).** List FOUR greenhouse gases.
(ii). State the sources of environmental impact of any two in (ci) above. [3 Marks]

**Question 6(ai).** State TWO properties of water that are different from the hydrides of Group 16.
(ii). Why are the first ionization energies of the d-block metals greater than those of the s-block metals? [4 Marks]

**(bi).** List THREE types of hydrides and give example of each.
(ii). Give balanced chemical equations for the reaction of two types of hydrides in water. [5 Marks]

**(c).** Name the ore from which aluminium can be extracted. [1 Mark]

---

**Answers — CHM 003 (2020):**

**(5ai).**
(a). NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) [½ Mark]
(b). SO₃(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₄(aq) [½ Mark]
(c). Al₂O₃(s) + H₂O(l) → No reaction [½ Mark]
(d). Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) [½ Mark]

**(ii).**
(a). pH = 7 (neutral) [½ Mark]
(b). pH < 7 (acidic) [½ Mark]
(c). pH = 7 (neutral) [½ Mark]
(d). pH > 7 (alkaline) [½ Mark]

**(bi).** The solubility of Group 2 elements decreases down the group due to a decrease in hydration and lattice energies. [2 Marks]
(ii). BaSO₄ < SrSO₄ < CaSO₄ < MgSO₄ < BeSO₄ [1 Mark]

**(ci).** CO₂, CH₄, chlorofluorocarbon (CFC), H₂O and N₂O. [2 Marks]
(ii). CO₂ — deforestation and combustion of fossil fuel.
CH₄ — rice fields, landfills, leaking gas pipes, solid and organic wastes, termite mound and swamps.
CFC — refrigerators, aerosol propellants and air conditioners.
H₂O — transpiration, sublimation, atmosphere and condensation. [1 Mark]

**(6ai). Properties of water different from Group 16 hydrides:**
- smaller sizes and higher nuclear charges [1 Mark]
- the first electron is normally removed from the partially filled d-orbitals [1 Mark]

**(ii).** Because the d-block metals have: smaller sizes and higher nuclear charges; which required higher energy than the s-block metals. [1 Mark]

**(bi). Types of hydrides:**
Covalent hydrides — NH₃, H₂O, HCl, H₂S, PH₃ [1 Mark]
Ionic/saline hydrides — KH, NaH, CaH₂, LiH, AlH₃ [1 Mark]
Interstitial hydrides — TiH₁.₅, KaH₂.₈₇ [1 Mark]

(ii). KH + H₂O → KOH + H₂; NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄OH [2 Marks]

**(c).** Bauxite. [1 Mark]

### CHM 004: ORGANIC CHEMISTRY (2020)

**Question 7(a).** Give TWO differences between nucleophilic substitution unimolecular (SN1) and nucleophilic substitution bimolecular (SN2) reactions. [2 Marks]

| S/N | SN1 | SN2 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | It is a two-step reaction | It is a one-step reaction |
| 2 | Formation of an intermediate carbonium ion | No intermediate carbonium ion formed |
| 3 | Rate determining step is determined by concentration of both substrate and nucleophile | Rate determining step is determined by concentration of both substrate and nucleophile |
| 4 | Typical of tertiary alkyl halides | Typical of primary alkyl halides |
| 5 | Racemic mixture is formed | Waiden inversion takes place |
| 6 | Rearrangement may take place | No rearrangement takes place |
| 7 | It is a unimolecular reaction | It is a bimolecular reaction |

[2 Marks for Any Two]

**(b).** There are several isomers with the molecular formula C₅H₁₂O.
(i). Provide the structures and names of three unbranched isomers of the alkanol.
(ii). Which isomer(s) is/are chiral?
(iii). Write a chemical equation for each compound in (bi) with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and provide names for the products formed.

Glycine structure: NH₂—CH—COOH with H substituent
Alanine structure: NH₂—CH—COOH with CH₃ substituent

(i). Draw a structure of the compound formed when glycine is combined with alanine.
(ii). What class of compound is formed in (i) above?
(iii). What type of bond is obtained?
(iv). Draw the zwitterionic forms of glycine and alanine.
(v). An organic compound F, with the empirical formula C₅H₁₀O has a vapour density of 43.
(i). What is the molecular formula of F?
(ii). If F does not react with Fehling's or Tollen's reagent but gives a yellow precipitate when reacted with aqueous iodine, draw the structure and give the IUPAC name of F.
(iii). Methylbenzene can react with chlorine in two ways. The products formed in each case depends on the reaction conditions. [3 Marks]

**Answers — CHM 004 (2020):**

**(bi).**
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)(CH₃) [1½ Mark]
(ii). CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ [½ Mark]

**(iii). Oxidation reactions with K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺:**
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) → CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO (pentanal) → pentan-1-ol
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) → CH₃CH₂CH₂COCH₃ (pentan-2-one) → pentan-2-ol
CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) → CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (pentan-3-one) → pentan-3-ol [3 Marks]

**(8ai). Molecular formula of F:**
Molecular mass of F = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 43 = 86
[E.F]n = 86; [C₅H₁₀O]n = 86; 86n = 86; n = 1
Molecular formula of F = C₅H₁₀O [1 Mark]

**(ii). Structure of F = Pentan-2-one/2-pentanone:** [1 Mark]

**(bi). Structure of A and B (from methylbenzene + Cl₂):**
A = CH₂Cl-benzene (benzyl chloride) — via free radical mechanism (UV light)
B = Cl-CH₃-benzene (chloromethylbenzene) — via electrophilic substitution (AlCl₃) [1 Mark]

**(ii). Reaction of A and B with NaOH:**
CH₂Cl-benzene + NaOH → CH₂OH-benzene (then LiAlH₄) → CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (hexan-3-ol)
No Reaction for B-type [1 Mark]

**(iii). Reaction products:**
(a). CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (hexanone)
(b). CH₃Cl-benzene + NaOH → No Reaction [½ Mark each]

**(c). Increasing order of acidity:**
Pentanoic acid < 3-chloropentanoic acid, 4-chloropentanoic acid, 2,2-dichloropentanoic acid — 3,3-dichloropentanoic acid. Ethylbutanoate [2 Marks]

Justification: Negative inductive effect / Number of electron-withdrawing groups / Proximity or closeness of electron-withdrawing group to the functional group. [1]

## JUPEB 2020 —

subject: chemistry
question:
PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

### QUESTION 1: QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS

You are provided with the following:
Solution Y: A 0.10 moldm⁻³ of HNO₃
Solution Z: A 1.86 g of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O in 250 cm³ of solution
Methylorange indicator.

**Procedure:**
(i). Pipette 25 cm³ of solution Z into a clean conical flask. Add 2 or 3 drops of indicator.
(ii). Titrate against solution Y in the burette. Record your titre value.
(iii). Repeat the titration two more times and find the average titre value.

**From your result, calculate:**
(i). number of moles of solutions Y and Z used.
(ii). concentration in moldm⁻³ of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ in substance Z.
(iii). concentration in gdm⁻³ of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ in substance Z.
(iv). the numerical value of n in the formula. [10 Marks]

**Burette Readings:**

| | 1st Titration (cm³) | 2nd Titration (cm³) | 3rd Titration (cm³) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Final Reading | 30.10 | 32.00 | 30.00 |
| Initial Reading | 0.00 | 2.00 | 0.00 |
| Titre value | 30.10 | 30.00 | 30.00 |

Average titre value = (30.00 + 30.00)/2 = 30.00 cm³ [1 Mark]

**N.B.:** If the difference between the obtained average titre and the actual value is:
±0.2: 1 Mark is awarded
±0.3: ½ Mark is awarded
±0.4: 0 Mark is awarded

**(ii). Balanced equation of reaction:**
2HNO₃ + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + (n+1)H₂O + CO₂ [1 Mark]

**(bi).** 100 cm³ of Y contains 0.10 mole of HNO₃
30.0 cm³ of Y will contain 30 × 0.10/1000 = 0.003 mole of HNO₃ [½ Mark]

From the balanced equation: 2 moles of HNO₃ required 1 mole of Na₂CO₃
0.003 mole of HNO₃ will require 0.003 × 1/2 = 0.0015 mole of Na₂CO₃ [1 Mark]

**(ii).** 25 cm³ of Z contains 0.0015 mole of Na₂CO₃
1000 cm³ of Z will contain 1000 × 0.0015/25 = 15/25 = 0.06 moldm⁻³ of Na₂CO₃ [1 Mark]

**(iii).** Molar mass of Na₂CO₃ = 2 × 23 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 106 gmol⁻¹
Conc. of Na₂CO₃ (gdm⁻³) = Conc. (moldm⁻³) × Molar Mass [½]
= 0.06 × 106 = 6.34 gdm⁻³ [1 Mark]

**(iv).** 250 cm³ of Z contains 1.86 g of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O
1000 cm³ of Z will contain 1000 × 1.86/250 = 7.44 g of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O
Therefore, mass conc. of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O is 7.44 gdm⁻³

Mass Conc. of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O / Mass Conc. of Na₂CO₃ = Molar Mass of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O / Molar Mass of Na₂CO₃

7.44/6.34 = Molar Mass of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O / 106
Molar Mass of Na₂CO₃.nH₂O = 7.44 × 106/6.34 = 788.64/6.34 = 116.6 [½ Mark]

114.12n = 788.64 − 672.04 = 116.6
n = 116.6/114.12 = 1.022 ≈ 1 [½ Mark]
